2026-11-16_r1.title: New review of 12 RCTs says oral magnesium isn't a routine insomnia treatment. Does that match what you've seen?
2026-11-16_r1.text:
A review in the Journal of Dietary Supplements pooled 12 randomised trials of oral magnesium for sleep, with searches up to June 2026. The conclusion was that it shouldn't be treated as a routine insomnia treatment, because the effects were small and the studies were mostly small and mixed in quality. The one form that showed a modest benefit was bisglycinate.

A few things I took from it. Most trials used people who weren't checked for low magnesium first, so if you're actually low the picture could be different. Form and dose varied a lot between studies, which makes pooling them messy. And sleep onset seems to be where the evidence is weakest.

For those of you who take it for sleep, did you notice a real change, or did it fade after a few weeks? And if you stopped, what did you replace it with? I'm curious whether people here have had better luck with glycine or theanine.

2026-11-16_r2.title: How are you handling the 3 PM crash? Coffee count, lunch, walks, something else?
2026-11-16_r2.text:
I spent 10+ years in corporate before starting my own thing, and the 3 PM slump was the most predictable part of my day. Big lunch, back-to-back calls, fourth coffee, and then I'd be wide awake at midnight wondering why.

What finally helped me was boring. Lighter lunch, a 10 minute walk after it, no caffeine after 2 PM, and the same wake-up time on weekends.

With all the talk about 70 and 90 hour weeks, I'm curious what actually works for people here. Do you push through on chai and coffee, nap, or have you changed how you eat? Especially interested in people on late US calls.

2026-11-16_r3.title: We need 25 to 30 g of fibre a day and most of us eat around 12. What does hitting it look like on Indian food?
2026-11-16_r3.text:
Fibermaxxing is everywhere right now, so I tried to work out what 25 to 30 g a day looks like with normal Indian food instead of imported stuff.

Rough numbers I used: a guava or a pear is 5 to 6 g. A tablespoon of chia is about 5 g. 100 g of whole urad dal is close to 20 g dry weight. Oats are about 10 g per 100 g. Rajma, chana and sprouts are all good too.

The food isn't the hard part. Eating it every single day with office lunches and late dinners is where I fall off.

What's your daily fibre source that actually sticks? And did anyone here go too fast and regret it? I've heard the bloating is real if you jump from 12 to 30 overnight.

2026-11-16_r4.title: We launched a supplement brand 3 weeks ago and published a lab report for every ingredient. Here's what it did for trust.
2026-11-16_r4.text:
Some context. I worked in corporate for 10+ years and started SILT, a morning and a night drink mix for busy professionals. Before launch we decided to publish everything: the dose of each of the 19 ingredients, the studies, and a lab report for every ingredient. 293 lab checks so far, 0 failed.

What I learned:

People do read them. A pre-booker asked us on Instagram for the exact mg and IU of D3, B12 and K2, and that question only comes from someone who checks.

It shortens the trust gap. We had 1,870 pre-bookings before a single review existed, and the most common question was "how do I know what's inside?"

It's also a discipline on us. Once the reports are public, you can't quietly change a supplier.

With FSSAI tightening nutraceutical labelling and sites like Trustified publishing pass and fail results, I think this becomes table stakes in India within a couple of years.

Founders in consumer brands, what did you make public early that you were nervous about? Did it help or hurt?

2026-11-16_r5.title: Scuba diving taught me more about falling asleep than any sleep hack did
2026-11-16_r5.text:
I've done 70-odd dives. The thing nobody tells you about diving is how slow your mind gets underwater. You breathe slowly because you have to, and after a dive I'd sleep better than any night in the city.

Back on land with a desk job, my problem was never being tired. My mind just wouldn't switch off at 11 PM. What helped me copy that underwater feeling was slow breathing for five minutes in bed (long exhale, roughly 4 in and 6 out), the phone in another room, and the same wake time every day, even on Sundays.

I'm curious what your version of this is. Is there an activity that reliably gives you a great night's sleep afterwards, and have you found a way to get that at home?
